South Vietnam: 21,833 killed{{cite book|last=Clarke|first=Jeffrey|title=United States Army in Vietnam: Advice and Support: The Final Years, 1965-1973|publisher= Center of Military History, United States Army|year=1988|url=https://history.army.mil/html/books/091/91-3/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120913060006/http://www.history.army.mil/html/books/091/91-3/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 13, 2012|isbn=978-1518612619}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|275}} | casualties2 = | yearcost1 = }} {{Campaignbox Vietnam War}} The inauguration of [[Richard Nixon]] in January led to a reevaluation of the U.S. role in the war. U.S. forces peaked at 543,000 in April. U.S. military strategy remained relatively unchanged from the offensive strategy of 1968 until the [[Battle of Hamburger Hill]] in May which led to a change a more reactive approach. The U.S. and [[South Vietnam]] agreed on a policy of [[Vietnamization]] with South Vietnamese forces being expanded and equipped to take over more of the ground combat from the departing Americans which began to withdraw in late June without any reciprocal commitment by the North Vietnamese. The morale of U.S. ground forces began to fray with increasing racial tensions and the first instances of [[fragging]] and combat refusal. The antiwar movement in the U.S. continued to grow and public opinion turned increasingly antiwar when the [[Mỹ Lai massacre]] was revealed in November. ==January== ;1 January to 31 August Operation Rice Farmer was a U.S. [[9th Infantry Division (United States)|9th Infantry Division]] and [[Army of the Republic of Vietnam]] (ARVN) [[5th Division (South Vietnam)|5th Division]] operation in [[Dinh Tuong Province|Dinh Tuong]], [[Kien Tuong Province|Kien Tuong]] and [[Kien Hoa Province]]s. The operation resulted in 1,860 PAVN/VC killed.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/resources/operations/operations.txt|title=Vietnam Archive Operations Database|publisher=The Vietnam Center and Archive|accessdate=10 November 2021}} ;1 January to 31 December [[Operation Quyet Thang II]] was an ARVN [[7th Division (South Vietnam)|7th Division]], [[9th Division (South Vietnam)|9th Division]] and [[21st Division (South Vietnam)|21st Division]] clear and search operation in [[IV Corps (South Vietnam)|IV Corps]]. The operation resulted in 37,874 PAVN/VC killed. ;3 January A [[Vietcong]] (VC) bomb exploded in a messhall at [[Củ Chi Base Camp]] killing 15 Americans mostly from the [[554th Engineer Battalion (United States)|554th Engineer Battalion]] and two Vietnamese kitchen staff.{{cite web|url=https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a955261.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200226032528/https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a955261.pdf|url-status=live|archive-date=February 26, 2020|title=United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam Command History 1969 Volume III|publisher=Headquarters United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam|date=30 April 1970|accessdate=25 June 2020}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|L-1}} ;6 January The [[South Vietnam]]ese Minister of Education, Dr. Le Minh Tri, was killed when two VC on a motorcycle threw a hand grenade through the window of the car in which he was riding.{{cite book|last=Willbanks|first=James|title=Vietnam War Almanac: An In-Depth Guide to the Most Controversial Conflict in American History|publisher=Simon and Schuster|year=2013|isbn=9781626365285}}{{rp|283}} ;12 January to 7 February In [[Operation Bold Mariner]] the [[2nd Battalion, 26th Marines]] and [[3rd Battalion, 26th Marines]] clear, search and depopulate the [[Batangan Peninsula]] a VC stronghold in [[Quảng Ngãi Province]].{{cite book|last=Smith|first=Charles|title=U.S. Marines In Vietnam: High Mobility And Standdown, 1969 |publisher=History and Museums Division, Headquarters US Marine Corps|url=https://archive.org/details/HighMobilityAndStanddown|year=1988|isbn=9781494287627}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|300–3}} ;14 January During [[Operation Toan Thang II]] a convoy of the 48th Transportation Group was ambushed in [[Tây Ninh Province]], 122 PAVN/VC were killed and three individual and one crew-served weapons were captured; U.S. losses were seven killed.{{rp|L-1–2}} ;18 January The parties to the [[Paris Peace Talks]] came to an agreement on the shape of the conference tables and the placement of the representatives who were negotiating an end to the war. After being delayed for nearly six weeks over procedural disagreements raised by South Vietnamese Vice President [[Nguyễn Cao Kỳ]], the parties came to an accord that "The two sides would be 'clearly separated' by two rectangular tables with a round one in the middle" and that the tables would have "no nameplates, no flags and no written minutes of the understanding" on the setup. ;20 January [[Richard Nixon]] is inaugurated as 37th [[President of the United States]]. ;21 January [[The White House]] issues National Security Study Memorandum 1 to the [[List of ambassadors of the United States to South Vietnam|U.S. Ambassador in Saigon]], the [[Joint Chiefs of Staff]] and [[Military Assistance Command Vietnam]] (MACV) "to develop an agreed evaluation of the situation in Vietnam as a basis for making policy decisions."{{cite web|url=https://www.nixonlibrary.gov/sites/default/files/virtuallibrary/documents/nssm/nssm_001.pdf|title=National Security Study Memorandum 1|publisher=Nixon Library|date=21 January 1969|accessdate=28 August 2020}}{{PD-notice}} ;22 January to 18 March The U.S. [[3rd Marine Division]] launched [[Operation Dewey Canyon]] to attack [[People's Army of Vietnam]] (PAVN) base areas in the [[A Shau Valley|A Shau]] and [[Đa Krông District|Song Đa Krông Valleys]] of [[Quảng Trị Province]]. The operation results in 1,617 PAVN killed while 130 Marines were killed.{{rp|50}} ;29-30 January An ambush patrol of Company C, [[1st Battalion, 7th Marines]] observed approximately 300 PAVN cross the Song Ky Lam River, 6 km west of [[Điện Bàn]]. The company called in artillery fire and then engaged the unit, with Company D, [[5th Marines]] joining the action. A search of the area at dawn found 72 PAVN dead.{{rp|91}} The first [[M551 Sheridan]] Armored Reconnaissance Vehicles arrived in South Vietnam and were deployed by the 3rd Squadron, [[4th Cavalry Regiment (United States)|4th Cavalry Regiment]] and the 1st Squadron, [[11th Armored Cavalry Regiment]].{{cite book|last=Starry|first=Donn|title=Mounted Combat In Vietnam Vietnam Studies|publisher=Department of the Army|year=1978|url=https://history.army.mil/html/books/090/90-17-1/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121216224119/http://www.history.army.mil/html/books/090/90-17-1/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 16, 2012|isbn=978-1780392462}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|143}} ==February== ;4 February to 19 April Operation Cheyenne Sabre was a [[3rd Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division|3rd Brigade, 1st Cavalry Division]] operation in [[Biên Hòa Province]]. The operation resulted in 600 PAVN/VC killed. ;10 February Kỳ announced that South Vietnam would negotiate a political settlement with the VC once the PAVN had withdrawn from South Vietnam.{{rp|286}} ;14 February A [[Gallup (company)|Gallup]] poll showed that 35% of Americans favor an immediate withdrawal from South Vietnam, up from 21%.{{rp|286}} ;17 February to 31 October U.S. Army and ARVN forces begin the multi-division [[Operation Toan Thang III]] to keep pressure on PAVN/VC forces in [[III Corps (South Vietnam)|III Corps]]. The operation results in 41,803 PAVN/VC killed and 3,299 captured, U.S. losses were 1,533 killed.{{rp|A-17}} ;19 February A bicycle bomb exploded in a shop in Truc Giang, Kien Hoa Province, killing six civilians and wounding 16.{{cite book|last=Pike|first=Douglas|title=The Vietcong Strategy of Terror|publisher=US Mission, Saigon|year=1970|url= https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/231/2311404008a.pdf|pages=93–115}}{{PD-notice}} ;22 February [[File:Marine Air Support Squadron 3 Marine carries a shredded Viet Cong flag after an attack west of Da Nang.jpg|thumb|right|A Marine carries a shredded VC flag near Da Nang]] The PAVN launched the [[Tet 1969]] offensive against U.S. military targets near [[Saigon]] and [[Da Nang]]. The attacks were quickly beaten off. In the attack on [[Bien Hoa Air Base]] the PAVN lost 264 killed and 87 captured while ARVN losses were 10 killed and U.S. losses were one killed. Around Da Nang the PAVN/VC lost over 500 killed.{{rp|101}} The PAVN attacked [[Tiên Phước Camp]] which was defended by the 5th Special Forces Detachment A-102 and [[Civilian Irregular Defense Group program]] (CIDG) forces. The base was secured the following morning for a loss of 1 U.S. and 54 CIDG killed.{{cite book|last=Stanton|first=Shelby|title=Green Berets at War: U.S. Army Special Forces in Southeast Asia, 1956-1975|publisher=Ivy Books|year=1999|isbn=978-0804118842|page=201}} ;23 February A PAVN rocket attack on [[Da Nang Air Base]] destroyed a 450,000 gallon fuel tank beside the base and damaged a Marine [[Grumman A-6 Intruder|A-6 Intruder]].{{rp|97}} PAVN sappers attacked [[Hill 327]] and the positions of the [[2nd Battalion 7th Marines]] northwest of the Hill, both attacks were beaten back with 18 Marines killed and 80 wounded while the PAVN lost 75 killed or captured.{{rp|100}} A PAVN sapper attack on [[Dầu Tiếng Base Camp]] resulted in 21 U.S. and 73 PAVN killed. The PAVN 271st and 272nd Regiments attacked [[Patrol Base Diamond I]] occupied by the U.S. 2nd Battalion, [[27th Infantry Regiment (United States)|27th Infantry Regiment]]. The attack was repulsed with artillery and gunship fire with an estimated 118 PAVN killed and two captured.{{cite web|url=http://www.fold3.com/image/268290656/#268290656/|title=General narrative description of the battle at Patrol Base Diamond on the night of 24 February 1969 and the morning of 25 February 1969|publisher=Department of the Army, Headquarters, 2nd Battalion, 27th Infantry|date=26 April 1969|accessdate=15 July 2020}} ;24 February - 10 March The ARVN [[2nd Division (South Vietnam)|2nd Division]] conducted Operation Quyet Thang 22 in Quảng Ngãi Province. The operation resulted in 777 PAVN/VC casualties.{{rp|287}} ;25 February The North Vietnamese Foreign Ministry on Radio Hanoi stated that the "South Vietnamese people" could attack U.S. forces "at any place on Vietnamese territory" and denied that there was any agreement not to conduct such attacks in return for the bombing halt.{{rp|287}} ;26 February A PAVN sapper attack on Củ Chi Base Camp destroyed nine [[Boeing CH-47 Chinook]] helicopters of the [[242nd Assault Support Helicopter Company]].{{cite web|url=http://aviation-safety.net/wikibase/wiki.php?id=148178|title=26 Feb 1969 Boeing CH-47A Chinook 66-19022|publisher=Aviation Safety Network|accessdate=1 August 2020}} ;27 February A PAVN rocket hit LCU-1500 while it was loading at the Bridge Ramp in Da Nang killing 13 crewmen. In Paris the U.S. stated that the Tet 69 attacks, particularly against civilian targets, breached the understanding behind the bombing halt.{{rp|287}} ;27 February - 20 June Operation Quảng Nam was conducted by the ARVN [[Vietnamese Rangers|1st Ranger Group]] in [[Quảng Nam Province]]. The operation resulted in 688 PAVN/VC killed.{{rp|287}} ;28 February - 2 March In the [[Battles of Nakhang#Fourth battle of Nakhang|Fourth Battle of Nakhang]] the PAVN [[316th Division (Vietnam)|316th Division]] overran [[Royal Lao Army]] (RLA) forces at [[Lima Site 36]] at Na Khang. The PAVN lost an estimated 250 killed and the RLA lost nine killed. The PAVN lost 26 killed while an entire RLA battalion was killed.{{cite book|last1=Conboy|first1=Kenneth|last2=Morrison|first2=James|title=Shadow War: The CIA's Secret War in Laos|publisher=Paladin Press|year=1996|isbn=0-87364-825-0}}{{rp|209}} ;28 February to 8 May The U.S. [[101st Airborne Division]] and ARVN [[1st Division (Vietnam)|1st Division]] launched [[Operation Massachusetts Striker]] to keep pressure on the PAVN in the southern A Shau Valley. The operation results in 223 PAVN killed and two captured while U.S. losses were 59 killed.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/F0311/F031100081690.pdf|title=Combat Operations After Action Report Operation Massachusetts Striker|publisher=Headquarters, 2nd Brigade, 101st Airborne Division|date=25 May 1969|accessdate=25 June 2020|page=6}}{{PD-notice}} ;28 February to 28 February 1971 The [[11th Light Infantry Brigade]] launched [[Operation Iron Mountain]] to attack PAVN/VC bases and logistics routes in southeastern Quảng Ngãi Province. The operation resulted in 4,589 PAVN/VC killed and 137 captured while U.S. losses are 440 killed.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010622.pdf|title=Operational Report - Lessons Learned, 23rd Infantry Division, (Americal), Period ending 30 April 1971|publisher=Department of the Army|date=15 May 1971|accessdate=25 June 2020|page=29}}{{PD-notice}} ==March == ;1 March to 14 April [[Operation Wayne Grey]] was conducted by the 1st Brigade, [[4th Infantry Division (United States)|4th Infantry Division]] in the Plei Trap Valley, [[Kontum Province]]. The operation resulted in 575 PAVN killed and four captured, U.S. losses were 106 killed and one missing.{{rp|288}} ;1 March to 8 May The [[4th Marine Regiment]] launched [[Operation Purple Martin]] against three PAVN regiments operating near the [[Vietnamese Demilitarized Zone]] (DMZ). The operation results in 347 PAVN killed and approximately 100 Marines killed.{{rp|58}} ;1 March to 14 August [[Operation Kentucky Jumper]] was a clear and search operation conducted by the 101st Airborne Division, 9th Infantry Division and ARVN 3rd Regiment, 1st Division in [[Thừa Thiên Province]]. The operation resulted in 317 PAVN/VC killed for the loss of 61 U.S. killed.{{rp|288}}{{cite web|url=https://vva.vietnam.ttu.edu/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010777.pdf|title=Headquarters MACV Monthly Summary August 1969|publisher=Headquarters United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam|date=10 December 1969|access-date=3 November 2021|page=52}}{{PD-notice}} ;1 March to August 1971 In the [[DMZ Campaign (1969-71)]] the 1st Brigade, [[5th Infantry Division (United States)|5th Infantry Division]] (Mechanized) assumed responsibility for the defense of the DMZ from the 3rd Marine Division as it withdrew from South Vietnam. ;2 March [[China|Chinese]] [[People's Liberation Army]] troops attacked Soviet border guards on [[Sino-Soviet border conflict#Battle of Zhenbao (Damansky) Island|Zhenbao Island]], marking a new low in relations between North Vietnam's principal allies.{{cite journal|last=Goldstein|first=Lyle|title=Do Nascent WMD Arsenals Deter? The Sino-Soviet Crisis of 1969|journal=Political Science Quarterly|volume=118|issue=1|date=Spring 2003|pages=53–80|doi=10.1002/j.1538-165X.2003.tb00386.x}} Village and hamlet elections were held throughout South Vietnam, largely free of PAVN/VC interference.{{rp|354}} ;2-4 March Nixon met Lodge and Kỳ and Paris and subsequently stated that further attacks would not be tolerated.{{rp|288}} ;3 March [[File:Destroyed PT76 tank at Ben Het.jpg|thumb|right|One of two PT-76s destroyed at Ben Het]] [[Ben Het Camp]] was attacked by the PAVN 66th Regiment, supported by armored vehicles of the 4th Battalion, 202nd Armored Regiment. Two [[PT-76]]s and one [[BTR-50]] were destroyed by U.S. [[M48 Patton|M-48s]] of the [[69th Armor Regiment|1st Battalion, 69th Armor Regiment]] in one of the few armored battles of the war.{{cite book|last=Dunstan|first=Simon|title=Vietnam Tracks-Armor In Battle|publisher=Osprey Publishing|year=1992|isbn=0891411712|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/vietnamtracksarm00duns}}{{rp|150–2}} ;3-4 March Company A, [[8th Infantry Regiment (United States)|3rd Battalion, 8th Infantry]] lost 21 killed fighting a PAVN battalion at [[Landing Zone Brace]] in the [[Plei Trap Valley]] approximately 44 km west of Kontum.{{cite web|url=http://www.shakenbakesergeant.com/vietnam/Wayne%20Grey.pdf|title=Combat Operations After Action Report for Operation Wayne Grey|publisher=Department of the Army|accessdate=15 July 2020}} ;4 March The Rector of Saigon University, Professor Tran Anh, was shot by VC on a motorcycle; previously he had been notified that he was on the "death list" of the "Suicide Regiment of the Saigon Youth Guard." ;5 March South Vietnamese Prime Minister, [[Tran Van Huong]], narrowly escaped assassination by a four man VC team as he was being driven to his home in Saigon. Huong's car was attacked by the VC who were wearing stolen Ranger uniforms, however Saigon police and ARVN troops opened fire and gave the driver time to accelerate and escape.{{cite news|title=S. Viet Premier Escapes Killers|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|date=5 March 1969|page=1}} The PAVN/VC fired seven rockets into Saigon killing 22 civilians.{{rp|288}} ;6-11 March [[United States Secretary of Defense|Secretary of Defense]] [[Melvin Laird]] and [[Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff]] [[Earle Wheeler]] visited South Vietnam.{{rp|288}} ;13 March Kon Sitiu and Kon Bobanh, two Montagnard villages in Kon Tum Province, were raided by VC; 15 persons killed; 23 kidnapped, two of whom were later executed; three long-houses, a church and a school burned. A hamlet chief is beaten to death. Survivors said that the VC explained that: "We are teaching you not to cooperate with the government." ;15 March to 2 May [[File:2.3 Marines pass a destroyed North Vietnamese truck south of Khe Sanh.jpg|thumb|right|2/3 Marines pass a destroyed PAVN truck during Operation Maine Crag]] The 3rd Marine Division and a regiment from the ARVN 1st Division launch [[Operation Maine Crag]] in the "Vietnam Salient" of Quảng Trị Province. The operation uncovered large amounts of supplies and resulted in 207 PAVN killed.{{rp|67}} ;17 to 24 March The 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment conducted [[Operation Atlas Wedge]] in the [[Michelin Rubber Plantation]], resulting in 335 PAVN killed and 11 captured for the loss of seven U.S. killed.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/340/3400121001.pdf|title=Combat Operations After Action Report – Operation Atlas Wedge|publisher=11th Armored Cavalry Regiment|date=10 April 1969|access-date=1 November 2020|page=8}}{{PD-notice}} ;17 March - 7 April [[Operation Raindance]] was a USAF interdiction bombing campaign to support RLA forces fighting the PAVN/Pathet Lao on the [[Plain of Jars]].{{rp|207–13}} ;18 March to 28 May 1970 [[Operation Menu]] was the codename of a covert [[United States Air Force]] (USAF) [[Strategic Air Command]] (SAC) bombing campaign conducted in eastern [[Cambodia]] from 18 March 1969 until 26 May 1970. The supposed targets of these attacks were PAVN/VC sanctuaries and base areas used for resupply, training, and resting between campaigns across the border in the South Vietnam. ;18 March to 28 February 1971 The [[196th Infantry Brigade (United States)|196th Light Infantry Brigade]] and ARVN 5th Regiment, 2nd Division launched [[Operation Frederick Hill]] to pacify the coastal areas of [[Quảng Tín Province]]. The operation results in 7,514 PAVN/VC killed and 133 captured, U.S. losses are 572 killed.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010622.pdf|title=Operational Report - Lessons Learned, 23rd Infantry Division, (Americal), Period ending 30 April 1971|publisher=Department of the Army|date=15 May 1971|accessdate=25 June 2020|page=22}}{{PD-notice}} ;18 March to 28 February 1971 The [[198th Infantry Brigade (United States)|198th Light Infantry Brigade]] and ARVN 6th Regiment, 2nd Division launch [[Operation Geneva Park]] to pacify Quảng Ngãi Province. the operation results in 2,337 PAVN killed and 67 captured, U.S. losses are 231 killed.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010622.pdf|title=Operational Report - Lessons Learned, 23rd Infantry Division, (Americal), Period ending 30 April 1971|publisher=Department of the Army|date=15 May 1971|accessdate=25 June 2020|page=25}}{{PD-notice}} ;20-31 March Operation Quyet Thang 25 was conducted by the ARVN 4th Regiment, 2nd Division in Quảng Ngãi Province. The operation resulted in 592 PAVN/VC killed.{{rp|288}} ;21 March A Kon Tum Province refugee center was attacked for the second time by a PAVN battalion using mortars and B-40 rockets. Seventeen civilians were killed and 36 wounded, many of them women and children. A third of the center was destroyed. ;22 March A Gallup poll showed that 32% of Americans favor escalating the war, 19% favor continuing the current policy, 26% favor withdrawal and 21% had no opinion.{{rp|288}} ;23 March to 3 April The [[3rd Battalion, 9th Marines]] and elements of the 1st Brigade, 5th Infantry Division launch [[Operation Montana Mauler]] against the PAVN 27th Regiment north of [[Firebase Fuller]] in Quảng Trị Province. The operation results in 271 PAVN killed, U.S. losses are 38 killed.{{rp|60}} ;24 March The VC attacked [[Tam Soc Base]] in [[Sóc Trăng Province]] killing two U.S. advisers from MACV Advisory team 71 and capturing another two, both of whom died in captivity. ;25 March [[John Lennon]] and [[Yoko Ono]] began their first [[Bed-Ins for Peace|Bed-In for Peace]] at the [[Hilton Amsterdam]].{{cite book|author= Kruse, Robert J. II|chapter=Geographies of John and Yoko's 1969 Campaign for Peace: An Intersection of Celebrity, Space, Art, and Activism|editor1=Johansson, Ola|editor2=Bell, Thomas L.|title=Sound, Society and the Geography of Popular Music|publisher=Ashgate|year=2009| isbn=978-0-7546-7577-8|pages=15–16}} ;28 March Mass graves of victims of the VC's [[Massacre at Huế]] were uncovered.{{rp|291}} ;31 March to 29 May [[File:Search and Clear, 1969 (15156845906).jpg|thumb|right|7th Marines search for supply caches during Operation Oklahoma Hills]] The [[1st Marine Division]] and ARVN 51st Regiment, 1st Division launched [[Operation Oklahoma Hills]] in southwest Quảng Nam Province. The operation resulted in 589 PAVN killed, U.S. losses were 43 killed.{{rp|116}} ==April== The number of American military personnel in Vietnam peaked at 543,000.Lewy, Guenther (1978), ''America in Vietnam'', New York: Oxford University Press, p. 146.{{Cite web|url=http://www.historyplace.com/unitedstates/vietnam/index-1969.html|title=The History Place - Vietnam War 1969-1975|website=www.historyplace.com|access-date=2018-05-03}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.pbs.org/battlefieldvietnam/timeline/index3.html|title=Battlefield:Vietnam {{!}} Timeline|website=www.pbs.org|access-date=2018-05-04}} ;1 April Laird announced that B-52 bombing missions over South Vietnam would be reduced by 10% due to reductions in the defense budget.{{rp|291}} ;3 April The [[U.S. Department of Defense]] announced that the death toll for American soldiers in the war had exceeded the 32,629 who had died in the [[Korean War]], based on 312 additional deaths during the week from March 22 to March 28 to bring the toll to 33,641.{{cite news|title=Vietnam Deaths Surpass Korea|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|date=4 April 1969|page=3}} Laird announced that the U.S. sought to "Vietnamize" the war as quickly as possible but that troop withdrawals would not take place while the PAVN/VC was conducting attacks.{{rp|291}} ;4 April A pagoda in Quảng Nam Province was dynamited by the VC, killing four persons, wounding 14. ;5 April [[COSVN]] issued Directive 55 to all of its subordinate units, renouncing the strategy that had led to the Tet Offensive, saying: "Never again and under no circumstances are we going to risk our entire military force for just such an offensive. On the contrary, we should endeavor to preserve our military potential for future campaigns."{{cite book|last=Hoang|first=Ngoc Lung|title=Indochina Monographs The General Offensives of 1968–69|publisher=General Research Corporation|year=1978|page=118}} ;6-20 April Operation Muskogee Meadows was a [[5th Marine Regiment]] clear and search operation in Quảng Nam Province. The operation resulted in 162 PAVN/VC and 16 Marines killed.{{rp|117–8}} ;7 April [[Leaders of South Vietnam|South Vietnamese President]] [[Nguyễn Văn Thiệu]] announced that once PAVN forces were withdrawn from South Vietnam, former VC could participate in the political process but not as part of the VC or any other communist organization. This was rejected the next day by a VC spokesman in Paris.{{rp|292}} ;9 April VC attacked the Phu Binh refugee center, Quảng Ngãi Province and set fire to 70 houses, leaving 200 homeless. Four persons were kidnaped. A Gallup poll found that 44% approved of Nixon's handling of the war, 26% disapproved and 30% gave no opinion.{{rp|293}} ;10 April National Security Study Memorandum 36 required an interagency plan with specific timetables for turning over the war to the South Vietnamese on the basis of four alternative timetables (18, 24, 30 and 42 months), with a starting date of 1 July 1969.{{cite book|last=Hartsook|first=Elisabeth|title=The Air Force in Vietnam The Administration emphasizes air power 1969|publisher=Office of Air Force History|year=1971|url=https://media.defense.gov/2011/Mar/23/2001330099/-1/-1/0/AFD-110323-012.pdf|isbn=9781508981824}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|56}} ;14 April A PAVN/VC attack on [[Patrol Base Diamond III]] was repulsed with 198 PAVN/VC killed and eight captured and 40 individual and 42 crew-served weapons captured; U.S. losses were 13 killed.{{cite web|url=https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/504193.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019191636/https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/504193.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 19, 2020|title=Operational Report Lessons Learned Period Ending 30 April 1969|publisher=Headquarters 25th Infantry Division Artillery|date=19 August 1969|accessdate=30 September 2020|page=7}}{{PD-notice}}{{cite web|url=https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a955261.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200226032528/https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a955261.pdf|url-status=live|archive-date=February 26, 2020|title=United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam Command History 1969 Volume III|publisher=Headquarters United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam|date=30 April 1970|accessdate=1 October 2020|page=L-10}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|L-10}} ;15 April A VC armed propaganda team invaded An Ky refugee center, Quảng Ngãi Province, and attempted to force out the people living there; nine were killed and ten others wounded. ;15 April to 1 January 1971 The [[173rd Airborne Brigade]], ARVN 2nd Division and [[22nd Division (South Vietnam)|22nd Division]] and [[South Vietnamese Regional Force|Regional Force]] and [[South Vietnamese Popular Force|Popular Force]]s launched [[Operation Washington Green]] a security and pacification operation in [[Bình Định Province]]. The plane crashed into a school killing 24 at the school (most of them schoolchildren) and 10 of the 70 passengers.{{cite news|title=Crippled Plane Rams School in S. Vietnam|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|date=23 December 1969|page=1}} ;24-6 December The VC announced a three day Christmas truce, however Allied forces only observed a 24 hour truce starting at 18:00 on Christmas Day.{{rp|324}} ;26 December - 5 January 1970 The [[USS Starlight (AP-175)|SS ''Badger State'']] under contract to [[Military Sea Transportation Service]] and carrying a load of munitions bound for Da Nang had a bomb explode onboard causing a fire. The crew abandoned ship with 29 crewmen killed and the ship drifted before sinking on 5 January.{{cite web|url=http://www.usmm.org/badger_state.html |website=usmm.org|title=SS ''Badger State'' Rocked by Blasts|accessdate=25 August 2020}} ;28 December ''The New York Times'' published an analysis of a series of articles by Võ Nguyên Giáp published from 14 to 20 December in ''[[Nhân Dân]]'' where he outlined a move to better trained, highly mobile forces.
